entry: American [[Country music|country music]] singer and songwriter, born Virginia Wynette Pugh. One of the few singers to bring a woman's perspective to the male-dominated country music field, 20 of her singles topped the U.S. country chart. Her signature song "Stand by Your Man" drew both acclaim and criticism for its portrayal of women's loyalty to their husbands. Raised in Itawamba County, [[Mississippi]], she moved to [[Nashville, Tennessee]] in 1965. She recorded several number one singles with George Jones, whom she married in 1969. Wynette received two [[Grammy Awards]] and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame.

City on the Gulf Coast of [[Florida]], county seat of Hillsborough County (pop., 2020: 403,364). Its origins trace to Fort Brooke, established in 1824 soon after the United States acquired Florida from Spain. Rail service and cigar factories sparked rapid growth in the mid-1880s, and the historic Ybor City district reflects the city's Cuban and Spanish heritage. The economy is driven by healthcare, finance, technology, tourism and maritime trade, and Port Tampa Bay is the largest port in Florida. The city hosts the headquarters of United States Central Command, described as the most important military headquarters after the [[The Pentagon|Pentagon]].

Port city in northwestern [[Morocco]], on the coasts of the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and [[Atlantic Ocean]], and capital of the Tanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima region. Originating as a [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] trading center, it later became a Roman colony under the [[Roman Empire]]. In 1923 it became an international zone managed by several colonial powers and a destination for European and American diplomats, spies, writers and businessmen. That status ended with Moroccan independence, in phases between 1956 and 1960. Rapid modernization since then includes a business district and the Tanger-Med port, which is greatly benefiting its economy.

Partner and social dance originating in the 1880s along the [[Río de la Plata]], the border between [[Argentina]] and [[Uruguay]]. It arose in the impoverished port areas of both countries from a blend of Argentine milonga, Spanish-Cuban habanera and Uruguayan candombe. Tango was frequently danced in the brothels and bars of ports, where owners hired bands to entertain patrons. The dance spread worldwide and many variations now exist. Tango music typically features the bandoneon, violins, piano and double bass. On August 31, 2009, [[UNESCO]] approved a joint proposal by Argentina and Uruguay to include tango on its Intangible Cultural Heritage lists. The origin of the word remains disputed, with some theories tracing it to African sources.

Tracked, heavily armored fighting vehicle intended as a primary offensive weapon in front-line ground combat. Tanks combine heavy firepower, strong armor and mobility, typically with a large gun in a rotating turret. The name dates from 1915, when British *landships* were called tanks to keep their nature secret. The concept arose in [[World War I]] as a response to the stalemate of [[Trench warfare|trench warfare]], and the first tanks entered combat on September 15, 1916, at the Battle of Flers-Courcelette. Tanks became the backbone of [[Armoured warfare|armored warfare]] in [[World War II]], and the main battle tank concept developed during the [[Cold War]]. Modern examples such as the American [[M1 Abrams]] integrate composite armor and computerized fire controls.

Ship designed to transport or store liquids or gases in bulk. Major types include the [[Petroleum|oil]] tanker, the chemical tanker and the gas carrier, which carries liquefied natural gas. Chemical tankers carry products such as [[Ammonia]] and [[Chlorine]], while tankers also carry [[Wine]], [[Molasses]] and citrus juice. Tankers developed in the late 19th century, after iron and steel hulls and pumping systems made bulk liquid carriage practical. Oil spills from collisions and groundings have driven regulations such as double-hull requirements under international conventions. As of 2005, there were just over 4,000 tankers and supertankers of 10,000 LT DWT or greater operating worldwide.

Class of astringent, polyphenolic [[Biomolecule|biomolecules]] that bind to and precipitate [[Protein|proteins]] and other organic compounds, including [[Amino acid|amino acids]] and [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]]. The name refers to the abundance of these compounds in [[Oak|oak]] bark, which was used to tan animal hides into [[Leather|leather]]. Tannins are widely distributed in plants, where they protect against [[Predation|predation]] by acting as natural pesticides. Their astringency causes the dry, puckery feeling in the mouth after unripened fruit, red wine or tea. Molecular weights range from 500 to over 3,000 daltons for gallic acid esters and up to 20,000 daltons for proanthocyanidins. Their industrial uses include leather tanning and adhesives.

Chemical element (symbol Ta, atomic number 73), a very hard, ductile, lustrous, blue-gray [[Transition metal|transition metal]] named after Tantalus of Greek mythology. It is highly corrosion-resistant and always occurs in minerals together with the chemically similar [[Niobium]]. Its chemical inertness and very high melting point make it valuable for reaction vessels and vacuum furnaces. A thin, stable oxide layer enables its dominant use in [[Capacitor|electrolytic capacitors]], which provide high capacitance in compact volumes for portable electronics. Major production relies on ores from [[Australia]], the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and Rwanda, and it is being investigated for superconducting resonators in quantum processors. It was discovered in Sweden in 1802 by Anders Ekeberg.

Esoteric [[Yoga|yogic]] tradition developed in the [[Indian subcontinent]] from the middle of the 1st millennium CE, initially within [[Shaivism]] and Shaktism, and later in Buddhism and Vaishnavism. Tantric traditions view the body as divine, typically reflecting the union of [[Shiva]] and Shakti, and seek goals such as supernatural accomplishment, pleasure and kundalini ascent. The term also denotes a body of texts describing systems, methods and rituals. A key feature is the use of [[Mantra|mantras]], so in [[Hinduism]] the tradition is called *Mantramārga*, the Path of Mantra. In Buddhism, the [[Vajrayana]] traditions spread across Tibet and Nepal. Though Western views often equate Tantra with sex, scholars emphasize that sexual practices are rare and restricted to initiated adepts.

Blue to violet variety of the mineral zoisite, colored by small amounts of [[Vanadium|vanadium]]. It is found only in a small area near the Mererani Hills in northern [[Tanzania]], and it shows strong trichroism, appearing blue, violet or burgundy depending on crystal orientation. Rough stones are reddish brown and require heat treatment to bring out the blue-violet color. Tiffany & Co. named the gem after its country of origin and introduced it in 1968. In 2002 the American Gem Trade Association chose tanzanite as a December birthstone.

Ancient Chinese classic text traditionally attributed to the sage [[Laozi]] and regarded as the foundational [[Taoism|Taoist]] text alongside the [[Zhuangzi (book)|Zhuangzi]]. Its oldest excavated manuscript fragments, the Guodian bamboo slips, date to around 300 BCE, and the text likely took shape during the [[Warring States period]] (475–221 BCE). Its authorship and dating remain debated. The first biographical reference to Laozi appears in *Records of the Grand Historian* by [[Sima Qian]], a Han dynasty historian. Terminology from the text was reinterpreted by Legalists, Confucianists and Chinese Buddhists. It is organized into 81 short chapters of roughly 5,000 characters. First translated into French in the early 19th century, it is one of the most translated texts in world literature, next to the Bible.

Chinese poet and politician, one of the best-known poets of the Six Dynasties period. He spent much of his life in reclusion, farming, reading, drinking wine and writing poems on the pleasures and difficulties of life and his decision to withdraw from civil service. His simple, direct style was at odds with the literary norms of his time, and [[Song dynasty|Northern Song]] literati such as [[Su Shi]] praised him as a paragon of authenticity and spontaneity. He is regarded as the foremost representative of Fields and Gardens poetry. His fable *Record of Peach Blossom Spring* depicts an agrarian [[Utopia|utopia]] isolated from corrupt government. He later changed his name to Tao Qian, meaning *hiding*, after the Eastern Jin dynasty ended in 420, to signal his withdrawal from politics.

Source and fundamental principle of the universe, primarily as conceived in East Asian philosophy and religion. The Chinese character 道 means *way*, *path* and *road*, and philosophically *doctrine* or *principle*. According to the [[Tao Te Ching]], the Tao is self-existent, formless, eternal and the source of all existence, while all phenomena change continuously. Early texts distinguish the *named Tao* from the *unnamed Tao*, which cannot be expressed in language. The Tao is often described as feminine in the Tao Te Ching, a mother who gives birth to all existence. The concept is central to [[Taoism]], and related ideas appear in [[Confucianism]] and [[Mahayana]] Buddhism.

Form of [[Textile|textile]] art traditionally woven by hand on a [[Loom|loom]], usually to create images rather than patterns. Weft threads are usually wool or cotton, sometimes with silk, gold or silver, and they hide the warp in a weft-faced fabric. In late medieval Europe tapestry was the grandest and most expensive medium for figurative images, and it remained so in the eyes of many Renaissance patrons. Production centers in [[Flanders]] and [[France]] made large sets for the [[Nobility|nobility]] and clergy, often depicting hunts, biblical narratives or myths. The embroidered [[Bayeux Tapestry]] is a famous exception to the weaving technique. Surviving examples include the Hunt of the Unicorn series, c. 1495–1505, and the Apocalypse tapestries from Angers, c. 1377–1382, which illustrate the [[Book of Revelation]]. Modern workshops use Jacquard looms, though hand-weaving remains prized for its precision.

Large herbivorous [[Mammal|mammal]] of the family Tapiridae, similar in shape to a pig, with a short, prehensile nose trunk. Tapirs are one of three living branches of [[Perissodactyla]], alongside [[Horse|equines]] and rhinoceroses. They inhabit jungle and forest regions of [[South America]], [[Central America]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. Most tapirs are about 2 m long and weigh between 150 and 300 kg, with oval, white-tipped ears and four toes on the front feet. Tapirs migrated from North America into South America during the [[Pleistocene]] after the Isthmus of Panama formed. Four extant species are recognized, all classified as Endangered or Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, and tapirs became extinct in North America about 12,000 years ago.

Dark brown or black viscous liquid of [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]] and free carbon, obtained by destructive distillation of wood, coal, petroleum or peat. Since prehistoric times wood tar has been used as a water-repellent coating for boats, ships, sails and roofs. [[Sweden]] exported 13,000 barrels in 1615 and 227,000 barrels in its peak year of 1863, and the [[Royal Navy]] was the largest user. Demand declined with the advent of iron and steel ships, and production nearly stopped in the early 20th century. Coal tar, a byproduct of [[Coke (fuel)|coke]] production, is refined into [[Creosote|creosote]] and pitch for roofing and road paving.

American sports commentator and former competitive [[Figure skating|figure skater]]. She was the 1997 U.S. national champion and world champion, and the 1998 Olympic champion in women's singles. She is the youngest single skater ever to win the Olympic and World titles, and she was the first woman to complete a triple loop–triple loop combination in competition. Lipinski retired from competition in 1998, performed in live shows and retired from skating in 2002. In 2014 she became one of [[NBC]]'s primary figure skating commentators.

Canadian-American actress known for voice work in animation, websites and video games, born Tara Lyn Charendoff in [[Toronto]]. Her voice roles include Bubbles in *The Powerpuff Girls*, Timmy Turner in *The Fairly OddParents*, *Teen Titans*, *Ben 10* and *Rugrats*. She also voiced characters in the video games *Final Fantasy X* and *Final Fantasy X-2*, and her work on the latter earned an award from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences. Her first major animated role was the title character in *Hello Kitty's Furry Tale Theater*, which aired in 1987.

Large, often hairy [[Spider|spider]] of the family Theraphosidae, with more than 1,000 species in almost 200 genera. Many New World species carry urticating hairs that irritate the skin and, in extreme cases, damage the eyes. The largest is the [[Goliath birdeater]] of Venezuela and Brazil, reported to weigh 170 g with a leg span of up to 30 cm. Tarantulas inhabit savanna, [[Grassland|grassland]], [[Rainforest|rainforest]] and desert habitats, and most species are ground-dwelling burrowers. They do not use their webs for hunting, instead using them as building material or tripwire. Their venom is generally mild, comparable to a bee sting in potency for humans. Females often live 20 to 30 years in the wild, longer than most spiders.

Spider wasp of the genera *Pepsis* and *Hemipepsis*, among the largest parasitoid wasps. A female stings a [[Tarantula|tarantula]] to paralyze it, drags it to a burrow and lays a single egg on its [[Abdomen|abdomen]]. The hatching [[Larva|larva]] feeds on the still-living spider, avoiding vital organs to keep it alive. Adults feed on nectar, and males do not hunt. Females are hesitant to sting, but the sting is extraordinarily painful. Tarantula hawks are found on all continents except [[Antarctica]] and Europe.

Ukrainian poet, writer, artist and political figure. Born into a family of serfs under Russian rule, he became a fellow of the Imperial Academy of Arts in [[Saint Petersburg]] and joined the emerging Ukrainian national movement. His association with the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius led to exile in [[Central Asia]], where he continued to paint and write despite prohibitions. His poetry collection *Kobzar* is regarded as the foundation of modern [[Ukrainian language|Ukrainian]] literature, and some compare his significance to that of [[Robert Burns]]. He wrote poetry in Ukrainian and prose in Russian, including nine novellas, a diary and an autobiography. Freed after the liberal reforms of Alexander II, he was barred from settling in [[Ukraine]] and died in Saint Petersburg.

Genus of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family [[Asteraceae]], commonly known as dandelions. Its name derives from the Arabic *tarakhshaqūn*, meaning *bitter herb*. They are tap-rooted perennial herbs with a basal rosette of leaves, and their stems exude milky latex when broken. The genus has a near-cosmopolitan distribution, absent only from tropical and polar areas. The common dandelion, *T. officinale*, is native to [[Eurasia]] but is now widespread in North America. Dandelions are among the most vital early spring nectar sources for many [[Pollination|pollinators]]. Many species reproduce by apomixis, producing seeds without pollination that are genetically identical to the parent plant. Some species, such as the rubber-producing *T. kok-saghyz*, yield [[Natural rubber|natural rubber]] from their latex.

Earth-filled dam on the [[Indus River]] in [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]], [[Pakistan]], about 105 km northwest of [[Islamabad]]. Completed in 1976, it is the largest earth-filled dam in the world, standing 143 m above the riverbed. Its reservoir, Tarbela Lake, stores water for irrigation, flood control and [[Hydropower|hydroelectric]] power, with a storage capacity of 11.9 billion cubic meters. The installed capacity of 4,888 MW is to rise to 6,418 MW after a planned fifth extension financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the World Bank.

Phylum of microscopic eight-legged animals, also known as water bears or moss piglets. About 0.5 mm long, tardigrades have four pairs of clawed legs and live in [[Moss|moss]], [[Lichen|lichens]] and habitats from mountaintops to the deep sea. Among the most resilient animals known, they survive extreme temperatures, pressures, radiation, dehydration and starvation, and they have survived exposure to [[Outer space|outer space]]. In a dormant state called cryptobiosis, they can lose up to 97% of their body water. Their fossil record dates to the [[Cambrian]], some 500 million years ago. About 1,500 species are known, and they are studied as model organisms for resilience.

American retail corporation and discount department store chain headquartered in [[Minneapolis]], Minnesota. John Geisse and Douglas Dayton launched the first Target store in Roseville, Minnesota, in 1962, as an alternative to traditional discounters such as [[Walmart]]. It focuses on upscale, trending merchandise at lower costs, and its logo refers to the center of a shooting target, with a dog mascot named Bullseye. The company was renamed Target Corporation in 2000 and is a component of the S&P 500 Index. In 2013 a data breach exposed the credit and debit card details of 40 million customers.
